name: Loratadine
summary: A non-drowsy antihistamine that blocks the effects of histamine to relieve allergy symptoms, including those of allergic rhinitis and long-lasting hives. It can be bought from pharmacies and shops, drowsiness is its most common side effect, and a serious allergic reaction to it is rare but needs a 999 call.
usedFor: Symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis, the nose and eye symptoms of allergies such as hay fever
Symptomatic treatment of chronic idiopathic urticaria (long-lasting hives with no identified cause)
Relief of allergy symptoms in general, as the NHS describes it
howItWorks: The NHS says loratadine blocks the effects of histamine, a chemical the body releases during an allergic reaction. It is described as non-drowsy because drowsiness is less likely than with older antihistamines, although it can still happen. It eases the symptoms of an allergy rather than removing the allergy itself.
onset: The NHS says people may start to feel better within 1 to 3 hours of taking it.

common: Drowsiness is the most common side effect; the NHS says trying a different non-drowsy antihistamine may help.
The UK patient leaflet lists headache, increased appetite and difficulty sleeping as common effects in adults and children over 12, and the NHS notes children may get headaches.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert if drowsy.
serious: Rarely, a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to loratadine can occur; sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or struggling breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call, and the NHS says not to drive to A&E.
One UK leaflet advises contacting a doctor or a casualty department straight away after a skin rash or hives following the tablets.

Rare effects listed in the UK leaflet include dizziness, fits, rapid heartbeat, nausea, dry mouth, stomach lining irritation, hair loss and abnormal liver function, several of them very rare; a GP appointment, or NHS 111 if urgent, is the route to advice.

cautions: Pregnancy: the NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy but that a pharmacist or doctor is checked with first, while the UK SmPC says a large body of data shows no malformation or foetal toxicity yet prefers avoidance as a precaution.
Breastfeeding: the NHS says only very small amounts reach breast milk.

Medicines that inhibit the liver enzymes CYP3A4 or CYP2D6 can raise loratadine levels, and the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist before combining it with other medicines, including those bought without prescription.
People with rare inherited galactose or lactose problems are advised against the tablets.
Alcohol has not been shown to add to its effects according to the leaflets, but the NHS says it is best not to drink because it can cause sleepiness.
The NHS says long-term use is unlikely to do harm, but that it is best taken only for as long as needed.
monitoring: The sources retrieved describe no routine tests or monitoring for loratadine.

sections.heading: What is loratadine used for?
sections.body:
Loratadine is an antihistamine that the NHS describes as non-drowsy and as relieving allergy symptoms. In the UK its licensed uses, according to the summary of product characteristics, are the symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis and of chronic idiopathic urticaria. Allergic rhinitis is the medical name for hay fever and similar allergies that affect the nose, and urticaria is the medical name for hives. Chronic idiopathic urticaria means hives that last a long time without an identified cause.

The NHS says loratadine can be bought from pharmacies and shops and can also be prescribed. It comes as tablets and as a liquid medicine, and the NHS gives Clarityn as the brand name. The UK medicines database (emc) holds product information for the tablets and for the syrup, both under the Clarityn Allergy name.

sections.heading: How does loratadine work?
sections.body:
When someone meets something they are allergic to, the body releases histamine, a chemical that contributes to symptoms such as sneezing and itching. The NHS says loratadine works by blocking the effects of histamine, which reduces those symptoms. It eases the symptoms of an allergy rather than removing the allergy itself.

Loratadine is called non-drowsy because drowsiness is less likely than with older antihistamines. Even so, the NHS lists drowsiness as the most common side effect. The NHS says people may begin to feel better within 1 to 3 hours of taking it.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of loratadine?
sections.body:
Drowsiness is the most common side effect, and the NHS says trying a different non-drowsy antihistamine may help if it happens. The NHS says drowsiness happens in more than 1 in 100 people. If drowsy, the NHS advises not driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert. The NHS says children may also get headaches. The UK patient leaflet lists headache, increased appetite and difficulty sleeping as common effects in adults and children over 12.

Rarely, a person can have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to loratadine itself. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, very fast or struggling breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, skin, tongue or lips turning blue, grey or pale, sudden confusion, drowsiness or dizziness, or fainting. It also says not to drive yourself to A&E in that situation. One UK leaflet advises contacting a doctor or a casualty department straight away after a rash or hives following the tablets. The leaflet lists other rare effects, including dizziness, fits, rapid heartbeat, nausea, dry mouth, hair loss and abnormal liver function, and several are very rare.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, other medicines and alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy, but a pharmacist or doctor is checked with first. The UK summary of product characteristics reports a large body of data showing no malformation or foetal and newborn toxicity, yet advises it is preferable to avoid loratadine in pregnancy as a precaution. NHS 111 Wales says an antihistamine is usually recommended if one is needed in pregnancy. For breastfeeding, the NHS says only very small amounts of loratadine pass into breast milk.

Loratadine does not generally affect contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception, according to the NHS. The summary of product characteristics notes that inhibitors of the liver enzymes CYP3A4 or CYP2D6 can raise loratadine levels. The leaflet advises against the tablets for people with rare inherited galactose or lactase problems. The NHS suggests asking a pharmacist before combining it with other medicines, including ones bought without a prescription. The leaflets say loratadine has not been shown to add to the effects of alcohol, but the NHS says it is best not to drink because alcohol can cause sleepiness. On long-term use, the NHS says it is unlikely to do harm but is best taken only for as long as needed.

faqs.a: It is described as non-drowsy, because drowsiness is less likely than with older antihistamines. Drowsiness is still the most common side effect. The NHS advises not driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert if it happens, and says a different non-drowsy antihistamine may help.

faqs.q: Can loratadine be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy, but a pharmacist or doctor is checked with first. The UK summary of product characteristics prefers avoiding it in pregnancy as a precaution, despite reassuring data. The NHS says only very small amounts reach breast milk.

faqs.q: Does loratadine affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: According to the NHS, loratadine does not generally affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception. A pharmacist can answer questions about other medicines.

faqs.q: Is it harmful to take loratadine for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is unlikely to do harm if taken for a long time. It also says it is best taken only for as long as needed.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with loratadine?
faqs.a: The leaflets say loratadine has not been shown to add to the effects of alcohol. The NHS still says it is best not to drink alcohol, because it can make a person sleepy.
